Psychological perspectives.q: Two psychologists explain the same panic attack differently: one points to brain chemistry, the other to childhood memories. What does this show?
Psychological perspectives.right: The same behavior can be viewed through different lenses
wrong: One of the two psychologists must be wrong
Perspectives are different lenses, not right and wrong answers.
Panic attacks can only be explained by brain chemistry
Several perspectives can explain the same behavior.
Psychology has no agreed-upon methods for studying behavior
Perspectives are approaches to explaining behavior, not a lack of method.
Psychological perspectives.exp: Perspectives are like different pairs of glasses for looking at one behavior.

Psychological perspectives.q: Why do psychologists use several perspectives instead of just one?
Psychological perspectives.right: Each shows a different side of the behavior
wrong: Only one perspective can ever be correct, so they test all seven of them
Perspectives are lenses, not right and wrong answers.
Psychological perspectives.exp: Like looking through different sets of lenses.

The 7 perspectives.q: A student lists the perspectives for a quiz. Which one does NOT belong on the list?
The 7 perspectives.exp: The 7: psychodynamic, cognitive, behavioral, humanistic, biological, evolutionary, sociocultural.

The 7 perspectives.q: One psychologist says a fear of snakes was inherited from ancestors who survived by avoiding them; another says it was learned after a bad experience. Which two perspectives are these?
wrong: Psychodynamic and humanistic, focused on the unconscious and on growth
Neither is about ancestors or learning.
The 7 perspectives.exp: Ancestors' survival = evolutionary; learned experience = behavioral.

Psychodynamic perspective.q: A therapist says Tom's fear of commitment comes from feelings about his parents' divorce that he isn't aware of. Which perspective is this?
wrong: Behavioral looks at rewards and learning, not unconscious feelings.
Cognitive looks at conscious thought processes like memory and problem solving.
Sociocultural looks at culture, not unconscious feelings.

Psychodynamic perspective.q: Which explanation of a teen's nail-biting is psychodynamic?
Psychodynamic perspective.right: An unconscious conflict from early childhood
wrong: He gets attention from his parents each time he bites his nails
Psychodynamic perspective.exp: Psychodynamic: the unconscious mind and childhood experiences.

Cognitive perspective.q: A psychologist studies how students' ways of organizing information affect how well they solve math problems. Which perspective is she using?
wrong: Humanistic focuses on potential and free will.
Biological focuses on genes, hormones and brain chemistry.
Sociocultural focuses on culture and social influences.
Cognitive perspective.exp: Thinking, memory and problem solving = cognitive.

Cognitive perspective.q: A student keeps failing tests because she always assumes she'll forget everything. Which perspective focuses on that thought?
wrong: Behavioral, which looks at rewards and punishments she has received
The focus here is her thinking.

Behavioral perspective.q: A child keeps cleaning her room because her parents give her a sticker each time. Which perspective best explains this?
wrong: There is no unconscious conflict here, just a reward.
Stickers have nothing to do with ancestral survival.
The explanation is the reward, not her thought processes.
Behavioral perspective.exp: Behaviors that are reinforced by rewards get repeated.

Behavioral perspective.q: A dog learns to sit because it gets a treat each time. Which perspective explains this best?
wrong: Humanistic, about reaching one's full potential through free will

Humanistic perspective.q: A counselor helps a client set goals so he can become the best version of himself, stressing that he is free to choose his path. Which perspective is this?
wrong: Behavioral focuses on rewards, not free will and potential.
Nothing here involves the body or brain chemistry.
Nothing here involves the unconscious or childhood.
Humanistic perspective.exp: Full potential, free will and self-actualization = humanistic.

Humanistic perspective.q: Which word list fits the humanistic perspective?
wrong: Unconscious mind, childhood conflicts and hidden desires from Freud

Biological perspective.q: A researcher explains a teen's mood swings by changes in hormones and serotonin levels. Which perspective is this?
wrong: That would focus on culture, not body chemistry.
That would focus on potential and free will.
That would focus on thought processes.

Biological perspective.q: A twin study finds anxiety runs in families. Which perspective does this support?
wrong: Sociocultural, since families share the same culture and norms
The twin focus points to genes.
Biological perspective.exp: Genetics, brain chemistry, hormones and neurotransmitters.

Evolutionary perspective.q: Why do people fear snakes more than cars, even though cars kill far more people? Which perspective would say fearing snakes protected our ancestors?
wrong: Behavioral would point to learned rewards and punishments.
Psychodynamic would point to unconscious conflicts.
Humanistic would point to growth and potential.
Evolutionary perspective.exp: Behaviors that helped ancestors survive and reproduce = evolutionary.

Evolutionary perspective.q: Why might people prefer sweet, high-calorie food, according to the evolutionary perspective?
wrong: Their parents rewarded them with candy as children, building a habit
Evolutionary perspective.exp: Behaviors that helped ancestors survive and reproduce.

Sociocultural perspective.q: In one country people greet with a bow, in another with a handshake. Which perspective best explains the difference?
wrong: Greeting styles come from culture, not genes.
These customs differ by culture, not by ancestral survival needs.
Greeting customs come from culture, not unconscious conflicts.
Sociocultural perspective.exp: Culture and way of life shape behavior.

Sociocultural perspective.q: Teens in one country value independence, while teens in another value family duty. Which perspective explains the difference?
wrong: Biological, from different genes in the teens of each country
Sociocultural perspective.exp: Culture and way of life shape behavior.

Applying a perspective.q: A test asks you to explain why someone overeats using two perspectives. What is the best approach?
Applying a perspective.right: Explain it with what each perspective focuses on
wrong: Pick the one correct perspective and ignore the rest
The same behavior can be explained by more than one perspective.
Describe the behavior in detail without any theory
Applying means explaining it through a perspective's focus.
Name the perspectives without connecting them to the behavior
You must tie each perspective's focus to the behavior.
Applying a perspective.exp: Apply a perspective by using its focus (rewards, genes, culture, etc.) to explain the behavior.

Applying a perspective.q: To explain road rage from the behavioral perspective, what should you focus on?
Applying a perspective.right: What has been rewarded or learned
wrong: The driver's unconscious childhood conflicts and hidden feelings
Applying a perspective.exp: Apply a perspective using its focus.

Slide example: Suzanne.q: Suzanne loves romantic comedies. Which explanation uses the same perspective as your slide's example?
Slide example: Suzanne.right: Her friends all watch them, so it's what her group does together
wrong: Watching them releases dopamine and serotonin in her brain's reward system
She was rewarded with praise the first time she chose one
They remind her of unresolved feelings from her childhood
Slide example: Suzanne.exp: The slide's explanation is sociocultural: her culture and friends make romantic movies popular and social.

Slide example: Suzanne.q: Which explanation of Suzanne loving romantic comedies uses the humanistic perspective?
Slide example: Suzanne.right: They help her grow and feel positive
wrong: Watching them is popular among the women in her culture and friends
That is the slide's sociocultural explanation.
Slide example: Suzanne.exp: Humanistic focuses on growth and positivity.

Perspective keywords.q: A test question mentions "ancestors" and "reproduction." Which perspective is it most likely pointing to?
wrong: Its keywords are culture and social norms.
Its keywords are potential, free will and positivity.
Its keywords are thoughts, memory and problem solving.

Perspective keywords.q: A question mentions "social norms." Which perspective is it pointing to?
wrong: Cognitive, which is about memory, thoughts and problem solving
Its keywords are thoughts and memory.
Its keywords are rewards and learning.
Its keywords are genes and hormones.

Intuition.q: A coach picks players based on a gut feeling instead of their stats. Why would a psychologist distrust this?
Intuition.right: Understanding without reasoning is often wrong
wrong: Gut feelings are always based on careful research
Intuition is understanding without conscious reasoning.
Coaches are not allowed to use statistics
Nothing stops them; the issue is relying on intuition.
Intuition can only be used by trained psychologists
Anyone can use it; it just isn't reliable.
Intuition.exp: We can't rely on intuition, which is why psychology uses research.

Intuition.q: Which situation shows why we can't rely on intuition?
Intuition.right: Someone is sure a coin is "due" for heads
wrong: A scientist runs an experiment and repeats it to check her results
Intuition.exp: Intuition fails through misunderstanding probability, hindsight bias and overconfidence.

Why intuition fails.q: Which set of problems does your class say makes intuition unreliable?
wrong: Placebo effect, Hawthorne effect and Barnum effect
Those are problems with research studies.
Case studies, surveys and naturalistic observation
Those are measures of central tendency.

Why intuition fails.q: Which of these is NOT one of the reasons your slides give for intuition failing?
wrong: Hindsight bias, believing you knew it all along after the fact

Hindsight bias.q: After the election, Jordan says, "I always knew she would win," though he predicted the opposite. What is this?
wrong: Overconfidence is overestimating your knowledge before the fact.
That is seeing patterns in random data.
That is believing general descriptions apply specifically to you.
Hindsight bias.exp: "I knew it all along!" after learning the outcome.

Hindsight bias.q: After a team loses the championship, fans say the coach's strategy was obviously wrong. What bias might this be?
wrong: Overconfidence about how much one knows before the game starts
This is judging after the outcome.
Not about expectations of a treatment.
Hindsight bias.exp: "I knew it all along" after the outcome.

Overconfidence.q: Maya is sure she aced the test and doesn't check her answers, but she scores a 62. What best explains her certainty?
wrong: Hindsight bias happens after the outcome is known.
That is a result caused by expectations in an experiment.
That is answering to look good to others.

Overconfidence.q: Students predict they'll finish a project in 2 days, but it takes 6. Which error does this show?
wrong: Hindsight bias about having known the result all along
This is a prediction before the fact.

Misunderstanding of probability.q: After five coin flips land heads, Sam is sure the next one must be tails. What weakness of intuition does this show?
wrong: Hindsight bias is about claiming you knew an outcome after it happened.
That is changing behavior because you are watched.
Those are exact ways to measure variables.
Misunderstanding of probability.exp: Each flip is still 50/50; people are bad at judging chance.

Misunderstanding of probability.q: Which belief shows a misunderstanding of probability?
Misunderstanding of probability.right: A family with 3 girls is "due" for a boy
wrong: A fair coin has about a 50% chance of landing on heads each flip
Misunderstanding of probability.exp: Each event is still independent; people are bad at judging chance.

The scientific method (7 steps).q: A researcher has just tested her predictions and evaluated the results. What should she do next?
The scientific method (7 steps).right: Modify the theory based on her findings
wrong: Develop a theory for the first time
The theory comes before the hypothesis and testing.
Write the hypothesis before running any test
The scientific method (7 steps).exp: Observe, theory, hypothesis, test, evaluate, modify, replicate.

The scientific method (7 steps).q: What is the last step of the scientific method on your slides?
wrong: Develop a theory that explains what has been observed so far

Theory.q: After noticing that tired students seem to remember less, a researcher proposes a general idea that sleep supports memory. What has she proposed?
wrong: A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction made from a theory.
That is how a variable will be measured.
Theory.exp: A theory is a general idea that fits what you observed (step 2).

Theory.q: Which statement is a theory rather than a hypothesis?
Theory.right: Friendly people make others feel relaxed
wrong: Students with a friendly photographer will smile more in their photos
Theory.exp: A theory is a general idea.

Hypothesis.q: "Students who sleep 8 hours will score higher on tomorrow's memory test than students who sleep 4 hours." What is this statement?
wrong: A theory is a broad idea; this is a specific prediction.
A debriefing explains a study after it ends.
That is a number from -1 to +1.
Hypothesis.exp: A hypothesis is a testable prediction made from a theory.

Hypothesis.q: Which statement is a hypothesis rather than a theory?
Hypothesis.right: Kids who eat breakfast will score higher on today's quiz
wrong: Good nutrition helps the brain think more clearly in general over time
Not a prediction from a theory.
Hypothesis.exp: A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction made from a theory.

Operational definition.q: A study measures "aggression" as the number of times a child hits a doll in 10 minutes. What is this?
wrong: A confounding variable in the study
A confounding variable is an outside influence on the results.
A hypothesis is a prediction, not a measurement plan.
A case study examines one person or group in depth.
Operational definition.exp: It states exactly how the variable is measured.

Operational definition.q: Which is the best operational definition of "studying"?
wrong: Doing schoolwork in a way that helps you learn the material well
Operational definition.exp: Exactly how the variable will be measured.

Why operational definitions matter.q: Two labs run the "same" happiness study but get different results because each measured happiness differently. What was missing?
wrong: A larger control group of participants
Group size doesn't fix measuring the variable differently.
Consent is an ethics rule, not a measurement plan.
A p-value doesn't define how to measure a variable.
Why operational definitions matter.exp: Research can't be replicated without operational definitions.

Why operational definitions matter.q: In the senior-picture example, why does "smiling" need an operational definition?
Why operational definitions matter.right: People disagree about who is smiling
wrong: Smiling is impossible to see in printed yearbook photos at all
It can be seen; people judge it differently.

Replicate.q: A surprising finding is published. Other researchers run the identical study to see if they get the same result. What are they doing?
wrong: Debriefing explains a study to participants afterward.
That means defining how variables are measured.
They are repeating it, not making a prediction.
Replicate.exp: Replication checks that results are reliable (step 7).

Replicate.q: A study's result disappears when other labs repeat it. What does this suggest?
Replicate.right: The original result may not be reliable
wrong: The original study is now proven to be completely true and accurate
Replicate.exp: Replication ensures the reliability of results.

Three types of research.q: Which list names the three types of research on your slides?
wrong: Those are measures of central tendency.
Those are parts of an experiment.

Three types of research.q: Which type of research is the only one that can show cause and effect?
wrong: Correlational, which shows how two variables are related
Three types of research.exp: Only experiments can show cause and effect.

Descriptive research.q: A researcher watches and records how children share toys at recess, without changing anything. What type of research is this?
wrong: Nothing is manipulated, so it can't be an experiment.
She isn't measuring a relationship between two variables.
That combines the results of many studies.
Descriptive research.exp: Describing behavior (here by naturalistic observation) is descriptive research.

wrong: An experiment with a control group and a manipulated variable
Descriptive research.exp: Descriptive: case studies, surveys, naturalistic observation.

Correlational research.q: A study finds that students who use their phones more tend to sleep less. What type of research is this?
wrong: It relates two variables rather than just describing one.
A case study of one student
It studies many students, not one in depth.
Correlational research.exp: It shows a relationship between two variables.

Correlational research.q: A researcher finds that more exercise goes with better mood. What can she conclude?
wrong: Exercise definitely causes better mood in every person who tries it
Correlational research.exp: Correlational research shows a relationship between two variables.

Experimental research.q: A researcher wants to prove that caffeine CAUSES faster reaction times. Which type of research must she use?
wrong: Correlation can't show cause and effect.
Describing behavior can't show cause and effect.
Self-reports can't show cause and effect.
Experimental research.exp: Only experiments can show cause and effect.

Experimental research.q: To prove music improves focus, which design is needed?
Experimental research.right: Randomly assign some to music, some to silence
wrong: Ask students whether they think that music helps them focus
Experimental research.exp: Experiments manipulate variables to show cause and effect.

Case study.q: A psychologist spends two years studying one patient with a rare memory loss. What method is this?
wrong: Surveys question a sample of a group.
That watches behavior in natural settings, usually many people.

Case study.q: Why might a researcher choose a case study for a rare disorder?
Case study.right: Few people have it, so depth helps
wrong: To get a large random sample of the whole population at once
Case studies examine one person or group.
Case study.exp: A case study examines one individual or group in depth.

Case study: pros and cons.q: A researcher concludes all people with brain injuries react like the one patient she studied. What weakness of case studies is this?
wrong: Collecting too much data in a short time
That is an advantage of surveys.
That is a problem with observation.
That is a problem with surveys.
Case study: pros and cons.exp: Case studies can mislead if the person is atypical, and results can be overgeneralized.

Case study: pros and cons.q: Which is an advantage of a case study?
wrong: It can always be generalized safely to the entire population
That is a risk, not a strength.
Case study: pros and cons.exp: Advantage: in-depth information; illustrates general principles.

Naturalistic observation.q: A researcher sits in a mall food court and records how often people check their phones, without interacting. What method is this?
wrong: She is watching many people, not one in depth.
Naturalistic observation.exp: Observing behavior in natural settings without controlling it.

Naturalistic observation.q: What is the key rule of naturalistic observation?
Naturalistic observation.right: Don't control or manipulate the situation
wrong: Ask every participant to fill out a survey about their behavior

Naturalistic observation: pros and cons.q: During an observation, the shoppers notice the researcher and start acting more politely. What problem is this?
Naturalistic observation: pros and cons.right: Subjects acting differently because they notice the observer
wrong: A poor response rate because too few people send back the survey
Naturalistic observation: pros and cons.exp: One disadvantage: subjects may notice the observer and change their behavior.

Naturalistic observation: pros and cons.q: Which is an advantage of naturalistic observation?
Naturalistic observation: pros and cons.right: People act honestly in natural settings
wrong: It takes very little time and can be finished in a single afternoon
Naturalistic observation: pros and cons.exp: Non-invasive: subjects are more likely to show honest behavior.

Survey.q: A school sends a questionnaire to a random sample of 300 students about their study habits. What method is this?
wrong: A case study looks at one person in depth.
Students report on themselves instead of being watched.
Survey.exp: Self-reported attitudes and behaviors from a sample.

Survey.q: What makes a survey's results more likely to apply to the whole group?
wrong: Asking only the researcher's closest friends and family members
Survey.exp: Surveys question a representative random sample.

Survey: pros and cons.q: A survey asks, "Don't you agree that homework is a waste of time?" What disadvantage of surveys does this show?
wrong: It can be very time consuming to watch subjects
It studies only one atypical individual
It can't collect much data quickly
Surveys collect a lot of data quickly.
Survey: pros and cons.exp: The question pushes people toward one answer.

Survey: pros and cons.q: Which is an advantage of surveys?
Survey: pros and cons.right: Lots of data in a short time
wrong: People always answer completely honestly about their own behavior
Survey: pros and cons.exp: Advantages: large amounts of data quickly; flexible.

Correlation.q: A researcher wants to know whether hours of TV and reading scores are related, without changing anything. What is she studying?
wrong: Without manipulation, she can't show cause.
That is how a variable is measured.
That is a result caused by expectations.
Correlation.exp: Correlation describes the relationship between two variables.

Correlation.q: Which question could correlational research answer?
wrong: Does a new drug cause people's depression to go down?
What is one patient's life like?
Correlation.exp: Correlation describes a relationship between two variables.

Positive correlation.q: The more hours students practice piano, the higher their recital scores. What kind of correlation is this?
wrong: In a negative correlation, one goes up as the other goes down.
There is a clear relationship here.
Bimodal describes a curve with two peaks, not a correlation.

Positive correlation.q: Which pair is a positive correlation from your slides?
wrong: More absences from school, which go with lower grades
Positive correlation.exp: Both variables move in the same direction.

Negative correlation.q: As the number of absences rises, a student's grades fall. What kind of correlation is this?
wrong: In a positive correlation both move the same way.
The variables move in opposite directions.
Negative correlation.exp: One goes up, the other goes down.

Negative correlation.q: Which pair would most likely show a negative correlation?
Negative correlation.right: Hours of TV and homework completed
wrong: Hours of practice and skill, which both go up together
Negative correlation.exp: One goes up as the other goes down.

Zero (no) correlation.q: A scatterplot of shoe size and math grades shows dots spread everywhere with no pattern. What does this show?
wrong: That would show dots rising together in a line.
That would show dots falling in a line.
A scatterplot alone can't show cause.

Zero (no) correlation.q: What correlation coefficient means no relationship?
wrong: -1.0, which is the strongest possible negative relationship

Correlation coefficient.q: Which correlation coefficient shows the STRONGEST relationship?
wrong: Very close to zero, so very weak.
Correlation coefficient.exp: Strength depends on how close the number is to +1 or -1, not on the sign.

Correlation coefficient.q: Which coefficient is a weaker relationship than -0.5?
wrong: -0.8, which is further away from zero on the number line
Correlation coefficient.exp: Strength is how close it is to +1 or -1, not the sign.

Positive isn't \"good\".q: A study finds a positive correlation between stress and illness. A classmate says, "Positive, so that's good news." What is wrong?
Positive isn't \"good\".right: Positive only means both rise together
wrong: Stress and illness can't be correlated
They can be; the sign just shows direction.
The correlation must actually be zero
Positive isn't \"good\".exp: The sign describes direction, not whether it is good or bad.

Positive isn't \"good\".q: A study finds a negative correlation between exercise and illness. Is that bad news?
Positive isn't \"good\".right: No; more exercise goes with less illness
wrong: Yes, because every negative correlation is a sign of something bad
Positive isn't \"good\".exp: The sign describes direction, not good or bad.

Correlation does not equal causation.q: Cities with more firefighters have more fire damage. Which conclusion is best?
Correlation does not equal causation.right: A third factor, like bigger fires, may explain both
wrong: The study proves fewer firefighters would reduce damage
There is no relationship between the two
There is a relationship; it just isn't proven causal.
Correlation does not equal causation.exp: Like ice cream and sunburn, a third factor (big fires) causes both.

Correlation does not equal causation.q: Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together. What explains this best?
wrong: Eating ice cream makes people's skin burn more easily in the sun
Sunburns make people crave ice cream
It's a coincidence with no cause
Correlation does not equal causation.exp: A third factor (summer weather) causes both.

Population.q: A researcher wants her findings to apply to all U.S. high school students. What is "all U.S. high school students" in her study?
wrong: The sample is the smaller group actually studied.
That group doesn't receive the manipulated variable.
Population.exp: The population is the group the research is meant to apply to.

Population.q: A study samples 200 nurses to learn about all U.S. nurses. What is the population?
wrong: The 200 nurses who actually take part in the study itself
That is part of the sample.
Population.exp: The group the research is meant to apply to.

Sample.q: From all U.S. high school students, a researcher studies 500. What are the 500?
wrong: The population is all U.S. high school students.
That is the factor the researcher changes.
A case study examines one person or group in depth.
Sample.exp: The sample is the people from the population who take part.

Sample.q: Why do researchers study a sample instead of the whole population?
wrong: The sample is always much larger than the population being studied
Sample.exp: A sample is a variety of people from the population.

Representative (random) sample.q: To study students at her school, a researcher draws names from a list of every student. Why is this a good method?
Representative (random) sample.right: Everyone has an equal chance of being chosen
wrong: It guarantees the hypothesis will be supported
It lets her pick the students she knows best
It means she doesn't need a control group
Sampling and control groups are separate issues.
Representative (random) sample.exp: A random sample fairly represents the population.

Representative (random) sample.q: Which sampling method is most representative of a school?
Representative (random) sample.right: Drawing names from every grade at random
wrong: Asking only the students who happen to be in the library at lunch
Representative (random) sample.exp: Everyone has an equal chance of being included.

Experimental group.q: In a study of a new reading app, one group of students uses the app for a month. What is this group?
wrong: The control group doesn't use the app.
The population is everyone the study is meant to apply to.

Experimental group.q: In a caffeine study, which group is the experimental group?
wrong: The group that drinks plain water with no caffeine in it
Not a group in the study.
Experimental group.exp: The experimental group receives the manipulated variable.

Control group.q: In the same reading-app study, why does the researcher include students who don't use the app?
Control group.right: To compare them with the app users
wrong: To make the sample bigger without affecting results
The point is comparison, not size.
They are part of the sample.
The IV is manipulated, not measured.
Control group.exp: Comparing the groups shows whether the app really works.

Control group.q: A drug study finds both the drug group and the sugar-pill group improved equally. What does the control group reveal?
Control group.right: The drug may not really work
wrong: The drug works very well, since its group improved during the study
The control group improved just as much.
Control group.exp: Comparing the groups shows whether the treatment really works.

Independent variable (IV).q: A researcher gives some people 2 hours of sleep and others 8 hours, then tests their memory. What is the independent variable?
wrong: Age wasn't manipulated; it could be a confounding variable.
The room where the test is taken
That isn't what the researcher changes.
Independent variable (IV).exp: The IV is what the researcher manipulates.

Independent variable (IV).q: Does room temperature affect test scores? What is the IV?
wrong: Test scores, which are measured once the test is finished

Dependent variable (DV).q: A study tests whether room temperature affects test scores. What is the dependent variable?
wrong: That is held the same, not measured.
Dependent variable (DV).exp: The DV is what is measured; it depends on the IV.

Dependent variable (DV).q: Does sleep deprivation cause poor memory? What is the DV?
wrong: The amount of sleep, which is changed by the researcher
Dependent variable (DV).exp: The DV depends on the IV; it's what is measured.

Confounding variable.q: A study finds a new exercise plan causes weight loss, but the exercise group also ate healthier. What is the healthier eating?
wrong: The IV is the exercise plan.
That is a group, not an outside influence.
Confounding variable.exp: An outside influence that affects the results.

Confounding variable.q: Studying how exercise affects weight loss, which could be a confounding variable?
wrong: Weight loss, which is what the researcher is measuring at the end
Confounding variable.exp: Diet, sleep and genetics could confound the results.

Problems with research (all 11).q: Which of these is one of the 11 problems with research on your slides?
wrong: Those help research; they aren't a problem.
Problems with research (all 11).exp: Wording effects are on the list, along with placebo, Hawthorne and Barnum effects, and others.

Problems with research (all 11).q: Which is on your slides' list of problems with research?
wrong: Informed consent given by participants before the study begins
Problems with research (all 11).exp: Social desirability bias is one of the 11 problems.

Placebo effect.q: Patients given a sugar pill report less pain because they think it's medicine. What is this?
wrong: That is changing behavior because you're watched.
That is believing general descriptions fit you.
That is answering to look good.

Placebo effect.q: Why do drug studies give the control group a sugar pill instead of nothing?
Placebo effect.right: To account for the placebo effect
wrong: To make the control group feel guilty about not taking the real drug

Hawthorne effect.q: Factory workers work harder during a study simply because they know researchers are watching. What is this?
wrong: There is no fake treatment here.
Sampling bias in choosing the workers
That is about who is chosen to participate.
That is seeing patterns in random data.

Hawthorne effect.q: Why might observers hide behind a one-way mirror?
Hawthorne effect.right: So people don't act differently when watched
wrong: To make the placebo effect stronger in the group getting the drug
Hawthorne effect.exp: The Hawthorne effect: behaving differently because you know you're observed.

Barnum effect.q: Lena reads a personality reading that says "You sometimes doubt yourself" and thinks it describes her perfectly. What is this?
wrong: Nothing is being judged after an outcome.
This is a general statement that fits everyone.
Barnum effect.exp: Vague descriptions that fit everyone feel personal, like horoscopes.

Barnum effect.q: Why do horoscopes feel accurate to so many people?
Barnum effect.right: Their vague statements fit almost everyone
wrong: They are based on large, random, representative samples of people

Gambler's fallacy.q: A roulette player bets on black because red came up six times in a row. What error is this?
wrong: That is a result caused by expectations of a treatment.
That is about how questions are phrased.

Gambler's fallacy.q: A basketball fan thinks a player who missed five shots is now "due" to make one. What error is this?
wrong: Hindsight bias, which means believing you knew it all along afterward
This is a prediction, not hindsight.

Social desirability bias.q: On a survey, many students claim they never cheat, even those who do, because they want to look honest. What is this?
wrong: That is about who is chosen.

Social desirability bias.q: On a survey, almost everyone says they recycle every day. Which bias might inflate this?
wrong: Sampling bias, from asking only a narrow group of people
Even a good sample may overreport.

Self-report bias.q: A participant who guesses the study's hypothesis purposely answers the opposite way to mess it up. What problem is this?
wrong: That is about vague personality descriptions.
That is an outside influence, not a participant's choice.
That is "I knew it all along."
Self-report bias.exp: Participants trying to affect the outcome or being unrealistic about themselves.

Self-report bias.right: One who answers to help the researcher's hypothesis
wrong: One who simply forgets to fill out the survey before the due date
Self-report bias.exp: Participants try to affect the outcome or please the researcher.

Sampling bias.q: To show a new snack is popular, a company surveys only people leaving its own store. What problem is this?
Sampling bias.exp: The sample isn't representative of the population.

Sampling bias.q: A study of teen sleep uses only students from an elite boarding school. What is the problem?
wrong: The sample is much too large to finish analyzing in a short time
Sampling bias.exp: Sampling bias: failing to get a representative sample.

Wording effects (framing).q: More people support a policy described as "helping the poor" than one described as "welfare." What explains this?
wrong: The same people could answer differently based on the wording.
Nothing is judged after an outcome.
Wording effects (framing).exp: How a question is worded can skew answers.

Wording effects (framing).q: Which survey question is worded most neutrally?
Wording effects (framing).right: "How do you feel about the new lunch menu?"
wrong: "Don't you agree the new lunch menu is a total disaster for students?"
Wording effects (framing).exp: How a question is worded can skew responses.

Why ethics guidelines exist.q: Why can't some famous early psychology experiments be repeated today?
wrong: The reason on your slides is ethics.
They are famous; the issue is how they treated people.
Why ethics guidelines exist.exp: The APA set principles to protect everyone involved in research.

Why ethics guidelines exist.q: Who set the ethics principles for psychology research, according to your slides?
wrong: The DSM-5, the manual used to classify mental disorders
Why ethics guidelines exist.exp: The APA set principles to protect everyone involved.

APA ethical guidelines.q: Which of these is NOT one of the APA ethical guidelines?
APA ethical guidelines.exp: The guidelines: voluntary participation, confidentiality, informed consent, debriefing, no long-term harm, care for animals, institutional approval.

APA ethical guidelines.q: A study keeps data private, gets consent, debriefs, and was approved. Which guideline might it still be missing?
wrong: Confidentiality, keeping every participant's information private
APA ethical guidelines.exp: The guidelines also include voluntary participation, no long-term harm and care for animals.

Voluntary participation.q: A teacher requires every student to join a study or lose points. Which guideline does this break?
wrong: Debriefing is about explaining the study afterward.
That is about keeping information private.
That is about getting the study approved.
Voluntary participation.exp: People must choose for themselves whether to take part.

Voluntary participation.q: A participant wants to leave a study halfway through. What should happen?
wrong: She must finish the study, since she already agreed to take part
Voluntary participation.exp: People choose for themselves whether to take part.

Confidentiality.q: A researcher posts participants' names next to their depression scores online. Which guideline is broken?
wrong: That is about explaining the study before people agree.
That is about choosing to take part.
That is about explaining the study afterward.
Confidentiality.exp: Participants' information must be kept private.

Confidentiality.right: Using code numbers instead of names
wrong: Publishing every participant's name next to the results of the study

Informed consent.q: Before a study starts, participants read what will happen and sign that they agree. What is this?
What must happen BEFORE a participant joins a study?
wrong: Debriefing, which explains the full purpose of the study to them

Debriefing.q: After a study that used deception, the researcher explains its real purpose to the participants. What is this?
wrong: That is defining how variables are measured.

Debriefing.q: A study told participants it was about memory but was really about honesty. What must happen at the end?
wrong: Informed consent, which is gathered before the study ever starts

No long-term harm.q: A study plans to leave participants with lasting anxiety in order to test a theory. Which guideline does it break?
wrong: Even willing participants can't be harmed long-term.
The problem is harm, not privacy.
Approval doesn't make lasting harm acceptable.
No long-term harm.exp: Studies may not cause long-term physical or psychological harm.

No long-term harm.q: Which planned study would break the no-long-term-harm rule?
No long-term harm.right: One that leaves people with lasting fear
wrong: One that asks people to solve a short puzzle for ten minutes
No long-term harm.exp: No long-term physical or psychological harm.

Animal participants.q: A lab keeps its research rats in dirty, crowded cages without enough food. Which guideline is broken?
wrong: Animals can't give consent; the rule is about their care.
That applies to human participants after a study.
That is about human participants' privacy.
Animal participants.exp: All animal participants must be well cared for.

Animal participants.q: Which practice follows the guideline for animal participants?
Animal participants.right: Giving lab animals clean housing and food
wrong: Skipping care for the animals because they cannot give their consent
They must be well cared for.
Animal participants.exp: All animal participants must be well cared for.

Institutional approval.q: A student starts a study on classmates without asking any review board. Which guideline is missing?
Institutional approval.exp: Research needs approval from a research institution.

Institutional approval.q: Before a study begins, who must approve it, according to your slides?
wrong: Only the participants who have already agreed to take part in it
Institutional approval.exp: Research needs approval from a research institution.

Descriptive statistics.q: A teacher makes a chart of how many students got each letter grade to see the overall picture. What kind of statistics is this?
wrong: Those decide whether results apply to a larger population.
That measures how likely results are due to chance.

Descriptive statistics.q: Which is an example of descriptive statistics?
wrong: A p-value showing that a result is unlikely to be due to chance

Frequency distribution.q: A store clerk tallies how many customers fall into each age group. What has the clerk made?
wrong: That is a number from -1 to +1.
That measures spread around the mean.
Frequency distribution.exp: A count of how often each score or range appears.

Frequency distribution.q: A teacher counts how many students got each score from 0 to 10. What has she made?
wrong: A correlation between two different variables in the class
Frequency distribution.exp: A count of how often each score appears.

Histogram.q: The clerk turns the age tallies into a bar graph to spot patterns quickly. What is the graph?
wrong: A scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables.
That is a bell-shaped distribution, not a bar graph of tallies.
That is a relationship, not a graph type.
Histogram.exp: A histogram is a bar graph of a frequency distribution.

Histogram.q: Why use a histogram instead of a list of scores?
wrong: It shows cause and effect between the scores and other variables

Mean.q: Quiz scores are 6, 8, 10 and 12. What is the mean?
Mean.exp: Add the numbers (36) and divide by how many there are (4): 9.

Mean.q: Scores are 2, 3, 4, 5, 5 and 8. What is the mean?
wrong: 5, which is the score that appears most often in the list

Median.q: Ages in a group are 12, 15, 16, 19 and 40. What is the median?
wrong: That is not the middle value.
Median.exp: In order, the middle number is 16.

Median.q: Scores are 3, 8, 10 and 12. What is the median?
wrong: 8.25, which is found by adding the scores and dividing by four
Median.exp: Two middle numbers (8 and 10): average them to get 9.

Mode.q: Shoe sizes in a class: 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10. What is the mode?
Mode.exp: The mode is the number that appears most often.

Mode.q: A set has no repeated numbers: 1, 4, 6, 9. What is the mode?
wrong: 5, which is found by averaging the two middle numbers in the list
Mode.exp: The mode is the most frequent number; here none repeats.

Percentile rank.q: Jada is in the 70th percentile on the SAT. What does this mean?
Percentile rank.right: She scored higher than 70% of test takers
wrong: She answered 70% of the questions correctly
70% of people scored higher than her
Percentile rank.exp: The percentage of scores below hers.

Percentile rank.q: If you are in the 90th percentile, about what percentage of scores were higher than yours?
wrong: About 90%, because the percentile tells you how many beat you
Percentile is the share below you.
Percentile rank.exp: 90% of scores were lower, so about 10% were higher.

Measures of variation.q: Two classes both average 80 on a test, but one class's scores are much more spread out. What kind of statistic shows this difference?
wrong: Both classes have the same average.
Measures of variation.exp: Variation tells how similar or different scores are.

Measures of variation.q: Which is a measure of variation?
wrong: The median, the middle score when all the scores are put in order
Measures of variation.exp: Range and standard deviation measure variation.

Range.q: Test scores are 55, 70, 82, 90 and 97. What is the range?
Why is the range only a rough estimate of variation?
Range.right: One extreme score can change it
wrong: It uses every score in the set equally to describe the spread
It uses only the highest and lowest.
It's the same as the mode
Range.exp: Range = highest − lowest, a rough estimate.

Standard deviation.q: Class A's scores have a standard deviation of 3; Class B's have one of 15. What does this tell you?
Standard deviation.right: Class B's scores are much more spread out
wrong: Class B scored higher on average
SD shows spread, not the average.
Class A's scores are more spread out than Class B's
A smaller SD means scores are packed together.
Standard deviation.exp: Small SD = packed together; big SD = spread out.

Standard deviation.q: Why is standard deviation more useful than the range?
Standard deviation.right: It shows how scores spread around the mean
wrong: It uses only the single highest and lowest scores in the whole set
It counts the most common score
Standard deviation.exp: Standard deviation measures how scores vary around the mean.

Normal curve.q: Heights of adults form a bell shape with most people near average. What is this called?
wrong: That has a tail to the right.
That has a tail to the left.
Normal curve.exp: Most scores near the mean, fewer at the extremes.

Normal curve.q: On a normal curve, where do most scores fall?
wrong: At the two extremes, at the far ends of the curve
Fewer scores are at the extremes.
Only at the median of a skewed set
Normal curve.exp: Most scores fall near the mean.

The 68% and 95% rule.q: IQ has a mean of 100 and an SD of 15. About what percentage of people score between 85 and 115?
wrong: That isn't the rule for 1 SD.
The 68% and 95% rule.exp: About 68% fall within 1 SD of the mean.

The 68% and 95% rule.q: With IQ mean 100 and SD 15, about what percentage score between 70 and 130?
wrong: About 68%, which covers just one standard deviation each way

Outlier.q: In a town of teachers, one billionaire moves in. Which measure of income will change the most?
wrong: The mode stays at the most common income.
Outlier.exp: Outliers pull the mean the most.

Outlier.q: Why does your slide suggest using the median and mode in a town with one billionaire?
Outlier.right: The outlier pulls the mean up
wrong: The billionaire lowers the median income for everyone else in town
The mode becomes the billionaire's income
The mode stays the common income.

Skewed distribution.q: Most students finish a test in 30 minutes, but a few take over 2 hours, stretching the graph out on one side. What is the graph called?
wrong: One side has a long tail.
Skewed distribution.exp: A few scores stretch away like a tail.

Skewed distribution.q: How is a skewed distribution named?
Skewed distribution.right: By the direction of its tail
wrong: By the location of its highest peak, where most of the scores sit

Positive skew.q: On a very hard test, most scores are low but a few students score very high. What shape is the distribution?
wrong: The tail goes toward the high scores, to the right.
The scores bunch on one side.
Positive skew.exp: Tail to the right = positive skew, and mean > median > mode.

Positive skew.q: In a positively skewed set, which is largest?
wrong: The mode, which stays right at the highest peak of the curve
In positive skew, mean > median > mode.

Negative skew.q: On an easy test, most students score high but a few score very low. What shape is the distribution?
wrong: The tail goes toward the low scores, to the left.
The scores bunch at the high end.
Negative skew.exp: Tail to the left = negative skew, and mean < median < mode.

Negative skew.q: In a negatively skewed set, which is largest?
wrong: The mean, which gets pulled out toward the long tail on the left
In negative skew, mean < median < mode.

Symmetrical distribution.q: In a data set, the mean, median and mode are all 50. What does this tell you about its shape?
Symmetrical distribution.right: It is symmetrical, with no skew
wrong: Then the mean would be greater than the median.
Then the mean would be less than the median.
It must have two separate peaks, so it is bimodal
Equal measures point to symmetry, not two peaks.
A curve with a long tail that stretches out to the right side
A curve with a left tail
A curve with one tall bar

The mean follows the tail.q: A distribution's tail stretches to the left. Where will the mean be compared with the mode?
The mean follows the tail.right: To the left of the mode
wrong: To the right of the mode
The mean moves toward the tail, which is on the left.
The mode stays at the peak.
The mean follows the tail.exp: The mean always moves in the direction of the tail.

The mean follows the tail.q: In a skewed distribution, which measure stays at the peak?
wrong: The mean, which moves toward whichever side the tail is on
The mode stays at the peak.
The mean follows the tail.exp: The mean moves toward the tail; the mode stays at the peak.

Bimodal curve.q: A graph of customers by hour shows one peak at lunch and another at dinner. What kind of curve is this?
wrong: A normal curve has one peak.
Skew is about a tail, not two peaks.

Bimodal curve.q: A test given to two very different classes produces scores with two peaks. What should the teacher conclude?
Bimodal curve.right: There may be two distinct groups
wrong: The test was perfectly normal, with one big group of similar scores

Inferential statistics.q: A researcher wants to know whether her results from 200 students are true of all teenagers, not just chance. What does she need?
wrong: Those organize data; they don't generalize it.
That studies one person in depth.
Inferential statistics.exp: Inferential statistics decide whether results can be generalized.

Inferential statistics.right: Is this result true of all teens?
wrong: What was the average score in this one class of students today?
What is the most common score?
Inferential statistics.exp: Inferential statistics decide whether results generalize.

3 key principles.q: Which study gives the most trustworthy estimate of teen sleep habits?
3 key principles.right: A large random sample of teens nationwide
wrong: One teen studied in great depth
One person can't represent a population.
Hundreds of teens who all visit one sleep clinic
3 key principles.exp: Representative and bigger samples are better.

3 key principles.q: Which principle explains why one poll of 2,000 voters beats one of 20?
wrong: Fewer estimates are better than having many estimates to compare
3 key principles.exp: Representative, bigger samples and more estimates.

Meta-analysis.q: A researcher combines the results of 40 studies on exercise and mood into one estimate. What is this?
wrong: That studies one person or group in depth.
That collects self-reports from a sample.
Meta-analysis.exp: More estimates are better than fewer.

Meta-analysis.q: Which key principle does a meta-analysis put into practice?
wrong: Smaller samples are better because they are easier to control

The café example.q: Alex decides Café Mocha is better after asking two friends. What is the best criticism?
The café example.right: Her sample is small and unrepresentative
wrong: She asked too many people, making her data messy
Two people is far too small.
The issue on your slides is the sample.
She should have used a placebo
The café example.exp: Two friends each: unrepresentative and too small.

The café example.q: How should Alex improve her café study?
wrong: Ask the same two friends again, but with a longer set of questions
The café example.exp: Fix the unrepresentative and small sample.

Statistical significance.q: A study finds that a tutoring group scored higher, and the chance that this difference happened randomly is very low. What can researchers say?
wrong: The tutoring caused a huge effect
Significance doesn't tell you the size of the effect.
The results are due to chance
Low probability of chance means the opposite.
The study must be replicated before it means anything
It can still be significant now.
Statistical significance.exp: Low probability of chance = statistically significant.

Statistical significance.q: If a result is statistically significant, what can researchers reject?
wrong: The independent variable that they manipulated in the study
Statistical significance.exp: Low chance probability lets them reject the null hypothesis.

P-value.q: Which p-value gives the strongest evidence that results were NOT due to chance?
wrong: That is too high to be significant.
That means a 50% chance it was random.
That is very likely due to chance.
P-value.exp: The smaller the p-value, the less likely the result was chance; .05 or less is significant.

P-value.q: A study reports p = .03. What does this mean?
wrong: There is a 97% chance that the results happened by random chance
Small p means unlikely to be chance.
P-value.exp: A p-value of .05 or less is significant.

Effect size.q: Two studies are both statistically significant, but one raised scores by 2 points and the other by 15. What does the difference show?
wrong: A p-value says whether an effect exists, not its size.
Both can be significant with different strengths.
Effect size.exp: Effect size tells how strong the relationship is.

Effect size.q: Which tells you how big a difference is, not just whether it exists?
wrong: The p-value, which tells how likely the result was due to chance
That shows whether an effect exists.
Effect size.exp: Effect size measures the strength of the relationship.
